quests.instruction: Choose the strongest paragraph.
quests.prompt: An employee proposes that the company require two shared office days a week instead of three. Which paragraph has the best claim, evidence and explanation?
options: Two shared office days would keep the benefits of face-to-face work while giving staff more flexibility. The office has 200 desks and a new café on the ground floor. A third day adds commuting time without adding much joint work.
Three office days is an unfair burden on tired staff. In our team survey, 14 of 18 said most collaboration happens early in the week. It is cruel to make people commute even more.
Two shared office days would be better. In our team survey, 14 of 18 said most collaboration happens early in the week. Everyone else in the company would surely agree with this result.

Two shared office days would keep the benefits of face-to-face work while giving staff more flexibility. In our team survey, 14 of 18 said most collaboration happens early in the week. A third day adds commuting time without adding much joint work, so two days protects both goals.
quests.hint: Check that the evidence supports the claim, the explanation links them and the tone stays professional.
quests.explanation: The best paragraph offers relevant survey evidence and explains the trade-off. The alternatives overgeneralise, rely on emotion or use irrelevant detail.

quests.instruction: Which objection should the employee expect to be taken most seriously?
quests.prompt: The manager is reviewing a proposal to reduce office days from three to two.
options: The office has a limited number of desks on busy days, so staff might struggle to find a place to sit.
Junior staff may lose informal learning from sitting near experienced colleagues.
The office lease has already been paid for the year, so the company would waste money if it cut office days.
Some staff enjoy the coffee from the office machine, and many say it is the best part of the working day.
quests.hint: A serious objection concerns a real effect on people and on the goal of the policy.
quests.explanation: Reduced learning for junior staff affects the aims of office days. The other points are minor or unrelated.

quests.instruction: Choose the best concession and reply.
quests.prompt: Respond to the manager's concern about junior staff.
options: Junior staff do gain from working alongside colleagues, so the two shared days could be the same for whole teams, with mentoring calls on the other days.
Junior staff should be able to learn independently from online material, so no adjustment is needed to the two-day plan.
Junior staff matter most to the company's future, so all staff should be in the office for three days each week.
Learning happens everywhere, at home and in the office, so the number of office days does not really matter.
quests.hint: Accept what is valid and adapt the plan.
quests.explanation: This reply concedes the value of proximity and offers a practical fix. The others dismiss, overreact or minimise.

quests.instruction: Choose the position that best balances efficiency and access.
quests.prompt: A council wants to move routine services online.
options: Online services have benefits and drawbacks that councils should consider carefully before making any changes to the way they work.
Councils should keep paper forms because not everyone likes computers, and residents should not be pushed to change.
Councils can move routine services online if they keep a phone and in-person option for residents who cannot use digital services.
Councils should move all services online because digital is the future of public service, and residents will soon get used to it.
quests.hint: A balanced position takes a side and protects the people it might harm.
quests.explanation: This position supports the change and names a safeguard. The others are one-sided or avoid a position.

quests.instruction: Which evidence best shows that an online-only service could exclude some residents?
quests.prompt: Which evidence shows that some residents could not use an online-only service?
options: In a survey of 200 residents over 70, 68 said they had no reliable internet access at home.
Online forms are usually processed faster than paper forms, so residents get an answer in a matter of days.
Most residents in the town use the internet every day, and many of them prefer to do their business online.
The council's website was redesigned and improved last year, and it now works well on phones and tablets.
quests.hint: Evidence of exclusion must show who cannot use the service.
quests.explanation: The survey shows a group without access. The others do not concern exclusion or support the other side.

quests.instruction: What is the main weakness in this argument?
quests.prompt: 'Since 90% of residents used the online form last year, nobody needs the phone line.'
options: It attacks people who prefer the phone, by suggesting that they are old-fashioned and slow to change.
It relies on a sample that is too small, because it only includes people who happened to use the form.
It confuses cause with correlation, because it assumes the online form is the reason that people stopped calling.
It treats a majority as everyone and ignores the minority who may depend on the phone.
quests.hint: Ask who the 10% might be.
quests.explanation: Ninety percent is a majority, not everybody. Some residents may have no alternative.

quests.instruction: Choose the fairest and most specific thesis.
quests.prompt: A town is debating a curfew on amplified music at outdoor events.
options: Outdoor events should end by 10:30 p.m. on weeknights, with later finishes on a few agreed weekend dates, so residents can sleep while the town keeps its festivals.
Outdoor events and residents both have rights, so a curfew may or may not help, and the town should keep an open mind.
Outdoor events should finish whenever organisers choose, since festivals benefit the whole town and bring in visitors.
Outdoor events should end by 10:30 p.m. every night because residents matter more than festivals, and sleep should come first.
quests.hint: A fair thesis recognises both sides and still commits to a position.
quests.explanation: This thesis proposes specific times and balances residents and events. The others favour one side or avoid a position.

quests.instruction: Choose the best sentence for a letter to festival organisers.
quests.prompt: Residents want earlier finishes on weeknights.
options: We value the festival, and we ask that amplified music end by 10:30 p.m. on weeknights, as several residents with young children find later finishes hard.
Festival organisers clearly do not care about local families, or they would have shortened the hours by now.
The noise from your festival is a disgrace and must stop, because it has kept the whole street awake for three nights.
Please consider residents when planning future events, as noise is something that concerns a number of us on the street.
quests.hint: Combine respect, a precise request and a reason.
quests.explanation: The best sentence is polite and specific with a reason. The alternatives accuse, demand or are vague.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to complete the paragraph.
quests.prompt: 'Organisers argue that later finishes support local businesses. That is a fair point, and ____'
options: but businesses can find other ways to earn money, so a strict curfew would not do them much harm.
however, residents' sleep is more important than trade, so the curfew should apply to every event.
an extra hour on two weekend dates would give traders most of the benefit while limiting disturbance.
so the curfew should be removed for all events, because the town's businesses deserve the extra hours.
quests.hint: Concede and then propose a compromise.
quests.explanation: The correct ending accepts the point and proposes a limited change. The remaining options reject or dismiss.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest thesis.
quests.prompt: A company is considering unlimited holiday.
options: Unlimited holiday can work only if managers model taking leave and teams agree minimum cover; otherwise staff tend to take less time off.
Unlimited holiday is the best policy for employees, who will finally have real freedom over how they spend their time.
Unlimited holiday has strengths and weaknesses that companies should think about carefully before they make any decision.
Unlimited holiday is a trick to avoid paying for unused days, and staff should be cautious about accepting it.
quests.hint: The best thesis names the conditions for success.
quests.explanation: The best thesis takes a position with conditions. The others exaggerate, accuse or avoid a position.

quests.instruction: What assumption does the argument depend on?
quests.prompt: 'With unlimited holiday, staff will rest more, so productivity will rise.'
options: That holidays cost the company nothing.
That productivity is easy to measure precisely.
That staff enjoy their jobs more than other people do.
That staff will actually take more time off, not less.
quests.hint: What must happen for 'rest more' to be true?
quests.explanation: The argument assumes that unlimited holiday leads to more leave taken. If people take less, the conclusion fails.

quests.instruction: Which data would best test whether unlimited holiday leads to more rest?
quests.prompt: Choose the strongest evidence to collect.
options: Staff opinions of the policy collected in its first week, when most people are still getting used to it.
The number of other companies that have adopted a similar policy over the past few years.
The average number of days taken before and after the policy, by team.
The cost of the software used to record leave, compared with the cost of the old paper system.
quests.hint: The data must show actual behaviour over time.
quests.explanation: Days taken before and after directly measures the change. Early opinions, popularity and software costs do not.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest topic sentence for a paragraph proposing limited phone use in class.
quests.prompt: A school is debating phones in lessons.
options: Phones are part of modern life, so schools cannot ignore them any more, and lessons should be built around them.
Phones in class have advantages and disadvantages that are worth exploring, and teachers may wish to consider them.
Allowing phones only for teacher-approved learning apps could turn a distraction into a classroom tool, provided the rules are clear and enforced.
Students want to use their phones in class, and schools should respect students' wishes when they set the rules.
quests.hint: A strong topic sentence takes a position with a condition.
quests.explanation: The correct sentence proposes a limited use with conditions. The alternatives use popularity, preference or avoid a position.

quests.instruction: Which reply best treats the concern that some students cannot afford phones?
quests.prompt: The concern is about fairness.
options: Cost should not stop the school from modernising its lessons, so the plan should go ahead with phones as it stands.
Students without phones can simply borrow one from a friend for the lesson, so no special arrangement is needed.
Most students already own phones, so this is a minor concern, and the school should not spend time worrying about it.
That is a real equity issue, so lessons would use school tablets or shared devices for anyone without a phone, and no task would require a personal device.
quests.hint: Take the fairness concern seriously and offer a fix.
quests.explanation: This reply accepts the concern and provides a practical solution. The remaining options dismiss or minimise it.

quests.instruction: Choose the best revision.
quests.prompt: Original: 'Phones will make lessons amazing and fix boredom forever.'
options: Phones can make lessons better, and sometimes they may not, so it is hard to say what the overall effect will be.
Phones make lessons more interactive, which is good for learning, and this is why more schools are allowing them.
Phones could make some lessons more interactive, for example when students use a quiz app to check understanding, but they will not fix disengagement on their own.
Phones will make most lessons more engaging and will rarely cause any problems, provided teachers give clear instructions.
quests.hint: Replace overstatement with an example and a limit.
quests.explanation: This revision offers a specific example and admits a limit. The alternatives still overpromise or stay vague.

quests.instruction: Choose the most defensible claim.
quests.prompt: A shared building is deciding whether residents may use smart doorbells that record video.
options: Smart doorbells improve safety, so residents should decide for themselves what their devices record, inside or outside.
Residents should be allowed smart doorbells inside their own doors but not recording shared hallways, since hallway footage captures neighbours who have not agreed.
Smart doorbells are an invasion of privacy and should be banned from the building, whatever benefit residents may claim.
Smart doorbells raise privacy and safety issues that the building should consider, and residents should discuss them together.
quests.hint: A defensible claim sets a limit tied to a reason.
quests.explanation: The right claim allows the device but limits recording of shared space, with a reason. The others ban, permit everything or avoid a position.

quests.instruction: Which evidence best supports the claim that recording hallways can improve safety?
quests.prompt: Which evidence best shows that recording a hallway can reduce package theft?
options: Package thefts are annoying and inconvenient for residents, and many people have to collect parcels from a depot.
Cameras are a common feature of modern doorbells, and most models now come with night vision and a phone app.
After cameras were installed on one landing, reported package thefts fell from seven to one over six months.
Some residents say they feel safer when cameras are present, especially when they return home late in the evening.
quests.hint: Look for a measured change linked to the cameras.
quests.explanation: The fall in thefts after the cameras is measurable. The rest describe availability, feelings or annoyance.

quests.instruction: Choose the best reply to 'If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear.'
quests.prompt: A resident uses this argument to defend hallway recording.
options: Privacy is not only about hiding wrongdoing; neighbours can reasonably expect that their comings and goings are not recorded and stored by others.
Neighbours who object are probably hiding something themselves, since honest people are rarely troubled by being filmed.
Recording is only harmful when the footage is misused, so the important thing is to have rules about who can see it.
People who value privacy should live somewhere else, where the buildings do not use cameras in the communal areas.
quests.hint: The reply should challenge the assumption behind the argument.
quests.explanation: This reply corrects the assumption that privacy concerns imply wrongdoing. The others accuse, dismiss or accept the flawed premise.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest thesis.
quests.prompt: A national park is considering a small per-visitor levy.
options: National parks are national treasures, so visitors should be willing to pay a levy to help look after them.
A levy is the only way to protect the national park from the damage caused by large numbers of tourists.
A levy has advantages and disadvantages that the park should weigh before it reaches a decision about the plan.
A small per-visitor levy would fund trail repairs and rangers, provided local residents and school groups are exempt.
quests.hint: A strong thesis names the purpose and a fair condition.
quests.explanation: The best thesis links the levy to specific uses and protects access for some groups. The others exaggerate, use emotion or avoid a position.

quests.instruction: What is the weakness in this reasoning?
quests.prompt: 'Erosion is worst in summer, so tourists must be the only cause.'
options: It attacks tourists instead of giving a reason, and it assumes that visitors do not care about the park.
It offers only two options to choose from, and it ignores other reasons that might explain the damage to the trails.
It relies on a survey with too few people, and it does not say how the erosion was measured in the park.
Timing alone does not show tourists are the only cause, since weather and trail design may also matter.
quests.hint: A pattern in time does not identify a single cause.
quests.explanation: This answer notes other possible causes. The other options describe flaws not present.

quests.instruction: Choose the best reply to the concern that a levy will exclude lower-income families.
quests.prompt: A visitor levy could make the park harder to reach for low-income families. Reply while keeping the plan.
options: Free entry days, family discounts and exemptions for school groups would protect access while still raising funds.
Lower-income families can visit other parks if they cannot pay, so the levy does not reduce their choices much.
The levy is small, so it will not affect anyone, and there is no need to make special arrangements for families.
Families who care about the park will find the money to pay, so the levy will not stop them from visiting.
quests.hint: The best reply keeps the plan while protecting access.
quests.explanation: The best reply proposes specific measures. The others dismiss or assume.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest thesis.
quests.prompt: A shop offers a discount only to customers who use its loyalty app.
options: Shops that use apps are just collecting data to make more money, and customers should refuse to take part in it.
Shops should offer the same discount at the till, because requiring an app means customers must hand over personal data to get the price.
Loyalty apps are annoying, and shops should stop using them altogether, because customers should not have to install anything.
Loyalty apps have both benefits and drawbacks for shoppers, and shops should think about how best to use them.
quests.hint: The thesis should state the change and give a reason.
quests.explanation: The best thesis proposes a specific change and gives a fair reason. The alternatives insult, accuse or avoid a position.

quests.instruction: Which evidence best supports the claim that app-only discounts disadvantage some customers?
quests.prompt: Which evidence shows that some customers cannot use an app-only discount?
options: The shop's app has been downloaded 20,000 times, and most of the downloads were in the last year.
Loyalty apps track purchases to create personal offers, and they can suggest products that a customer often buys.
Many shops offer app-only deals during the year, and some of them run special offers on the app every week.
In the shop's own survey, 40% of customers over 65 said they do not use smartphone apps.
quests.hint: Evidence of disadvantage shows who cannot use the app.
quests.explanation: The survey shows a group who cannot access the discount. The rest describe the app.

quests.instruction: Choose the best revision for the shop owner.
quests.prompt: Original: 'Your app-only discount is unfair and greedy.'
options: The app-only discount excludes some of our regular customers, and I think that the shop should change the way it works.
Your app-only discount seems unfair to a number of customers, and I hope that you will think about changing it soon.
Some of our regular customers cannot use the app, so I would like to ask whether the same discount could be offered at the till.
It would be nice if the discount were available to everyone, because that would be a friendlier way to run the shop.
quests.hint: The revision should be polite, specific and constructive.
quests.explanation: The right revision names the problem and makes a request. The rest remain vague or blunt.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest paragraph.
quests.prompt: A student council argues for a student representative on panels that hire teachers.
options: Schools should include a student representative on panels that hire teachers. Students see daily classroom practice that an interview cannot show. Many other schools already do this, and it works well for them, so ours should too.

Schools should include a student representative on panels that hire teachers. Students see daily classroom practice that an interview cannot show. Some worry that students lack professional judgement, but a representative would add a view rather than cast a vote, so experience and student insight both count.

Schools should include a student representative on panels that hire teachers. Students are the people who are most affected by the decision. Anyone who disagrees clearly does not care about students, and their objections should be ignored.

Students should have a say in hiring teachers because they know best. Students see daily classroom practice that an interview cannot show. Nobody understands teaching better than students, so they should have the deciding vote.
quests.hint: Check for a claim, relevant support, a fair treatment of the objection and a respectful tone.
quests.explanation: This paragraph states the objection fairly and answers it. The remaining options use insults, popularity or overstatement.

quests.instruction: What is the weakness in the critic's argument?
quests.prompt: A critic says: 'Students would only pick the most entertaining teacher, so the idea is silly.'
options: It relies on a sample that is too small, because it is based on the opinions of only a handful of students.
It confuses correlation with cause, because it assumes that students who like a teacher must also learn more.
It dismisses the idea with an unfair caricature instead of answering the point that students would give input, not decide.
It offers only two choices, because it suggests that either students decide or they have no say at all.
quests.hint: Compare the critic's description with what is actually proposed.
quests.explanation: The critic exaggerates the proposal into 'students pick' when the proposal is for input. This is a strawman.

quests.instruction: Choose the best conclusion.
quests.prompt: The paragraph argued for a student voice on hiring panels, with the final decision left to staff.
options: Giving students a voice, but not the final say, would improve hiring decisions and show that the school takes their experience seriously.
Hiring panels have many members, and students are only one kind of possible member, so their role should be small.
This is only one idea, and there may be better ways to involve students, so the school could look into other options.
Students should decide who teaches them, because they are the ones who sit in the classes every day of the year.
quests.hint: The conclusion should match the argument's limits.
quests.explanation: The best conclusion restates the balanced proposal and its benefits. The others overstate, describe or retreat.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest thesis.
quests.prompt: A school is deciding whether to publish class exam-ranking lists. Which thesis takes a fair position and gives a reason?
options: Schools should share exam rankings privately with each student alongside personal targets, because private feedback keeps the motivation to improve while avoiding public embarrassment.
Exam rankings can help some students and hurt others, which is worth thinking about carefully before schools decide what to do about them.
Schools should stop publishing ranking lists altogether because they are cruel, and everyone knows that they make many students feel bad about themselves.
Schools should publish ranking lists because competition is good for all students, and it prepares them for the pressures they will meet later in life.
quests.hint: The strongest thesis has a clear position, a reason and a balanced view of the goal.
quests.explanation: This thesis acknowledges the value of motivation and offers an alternative. The remaining options are emotional, one-sided or avoid a position.

quests.instruction: Choose the best response.
quests.prompt: A parent says: 'Ranking lists motivate students by showing them where they stand.' Respond with concession, rebuttal and respect.
options: Motivation is not a good reason for publishing the lists, because the harm to weaker students is far greater than any benefit that stronger students might gain.
Many schools publish ranking lists, so there must be something in the idea, and it would be wrong to dismiss a practice that has lasted so long.

Some students may be motivated by seeing where they stand, and that matters; but a public list also exposes those who are struggling, so private rankings with targets would keep the motivation and reduce the harm.
Public lists motivate nobody, since students hate them, and any school that publishes them is ignoring what its own students say about the practice.
quests.hint: A strong response concedes what is valid, replies with a reason and offers a solution.
quests.explanation: This response accepts the motivation point, explains the harm and proposes an alternative. The alternatives dismiss, exaggerate or use popularity.

quests.instruction: Choose the best revision of the paragraph.
quests.prompt: Original: 'Ranking lists are cruel and everyone knows they ruin students. They are cruel because they make students feel bad. Nobody benefits from ranking lists.'
options: Public ranking lists can discourage students who are already struggling, and they show little about individual progress; private feedback and personal targets would motivate students without exposing them.
Public ranking lists are harmful and rarely help students, so schools should stop publishing them and look for other ways to raise standards.
Ranking lists make many students feel bad about themselves, which is a good reason for schools to stop using them and to try something new.
Ranking lists are unfair to students, and private feedback would be better for students, who would then feel more respected by their teachers.
quests.hint: Fix the overgeneralisation, the repetition and the missing reason all at once.
quests.explanation: The correct revision limits the claim, gives a reason and proposes an alternative. The other choices keep vague claims or repetition.
